title: Strangers and refugees
hookLine: you were strangers in Egypt: why the Torah grounds the welcome of the stranger in memory, and why the seder makes everyone remember
tomorrow: a saint preached to a crowd of birds. what did he tell them?

lines: THE TORAH COMES BACK TO HIM.
cards: A moving van. A family carrying boxes up the stairs. A kid standing alone by the mailboxes, reading every name on them.
The Torah comes back to people like that kid more than once. And it doesn't only say be kind to them. It adds a reason: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
Why remind a whole people that they were once the new ones?

teach.b: Go back to how they got there. Jacob's family came down to Egypt in a famine, hungry. Joseph, the brother they had once sold, fed them, and they settled.
For a while they were welcome.

teach.h: A NEW KING, WHICH KNEW NOT JOSEPH.
teach.b: Then, in the book of Exodus: "Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph." The newcomers became slaves. So when the Torah gives its law, it reaches for that memory.

teach.h: YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.
teach.b: "Thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You know the heart. That's the argument.
Not pity. Memory. Leviticus goes further: the stranger who lives among you shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself."

teach.h: THE SEDER: AS IF YOU LEFT EGYPT.
teach.b: And the Passover seder keeps that memory alive. Jewish families retell the slavery at the table, and the Mishnah says that in every generation a person should see themselves as if they had come out of Egypt.
Not great-great-grandparents. You. So you taste the bitter herbs.
That's the Jewish teaching: the memory of being a stranger is the ground for welcoming one.

how: At the Passover seder, Jewish families retell the slavery in Egypt and the Exodus, eat bitter herbs and matzah, and are taught to see themselves as if they had left Egypt. The command to love the stranger is often read alongside it.

practice: Take a pen and write one line by hand: you know the heart of a stranger. Under it, write a few words about a time you were the new one: a school, a job, a city. Stay with that memory for the rest of the sit.
